posts.reason: Rare hard evidence on agent-written code: a 35-hour, billion-token run with the actual excerpts it committed, and a thread of practitioners comparing how they keep such code maintainable.
A first-hand account of rebuilding a large public site's 70-plus components and 25 templates in plain native CSS, set against the old Zen Garden promise of separating design from markup.
Instead of speculating about a post-work future, it reads it off historical ethnographies of people who already lived without work, and lands on an argument about where dignity comes from.
Builds a backup system one failure at a time, naming each trade-off as it appears, and the thread adds expert corrections on snapshot consistency, ACLs and sparse files.
A vivid long read on the New Guinea highlands and their 1930 first contact, with a thread led by first-hand family accounts and expert corrections.
A short nudge from a conference speaker and MC, backed by a thread of speakers describing what silence and feedback actually feel like from the stage.
Argues that stepping into other teams' work can pay off, then separates that from two harmful kinds of empire-building: building in-house instead of buying, and duplicating central services.
One clear idea, that subtraction is the decision teams most often skip, with two examples of features quietly growing into rebuilt file managers and mail clients.
A tiny prompt that sets off a long, concrete thread comparing how languages from Lisp to Elixir name and order fold, filter and reject.
Pulls together about two dozen preference surveys since 1979, with their methodological limits, on the gap between what the public likes and what architects build.
